questions.q: What does transaction-based forecasting rely on?
options: Historical trends projected forward with no system transactions
Open, not-yet-settled transactions already existing somewhere in Oracle
Only bank statement balances from the last 24 hours
A fixed percentage of last year's revenue
questions.explain: Transaction-based forecasting uses open Payables and Receivables transactions (and similar) that haven't settled yet to project upcoming cash flow.

questions.q: For which kind of cash flow is trend-based (historical) forecasting especially useful?
options: Only categories with zero historical data
Only intercompany bank transfers
Only transactions already reconciled to a bank statement
Cash flow categories, like retail cash sales, that don't show up as a clean open transaction but follow a predictable pattern
questions.explain: Trend-based forecasting projects past actuals forward, which is useful for cash flows without a corresponding open system transaction.

questions.q: What do the 'rows' and 'columns' of a cash forecast template represent?
options: Rows are sources of cash flow; columns are time buckets like daily, weekly, or monthly
Rows are bank branches; columns are legal entities
Rows are currencies; columns are reconciliation rule sets
Rows and columns have no defined meaning in a forecast template
questions.explain: A forecast template defines which cash-flow sources (rows) and which time periods (columns) structure the forecast.

questions.q: What capability does Oracle Fusion Cash Management support for forecasting across a multinational company?
options: Forecasting in only one currency per company, ever
Forecasting is limited to a single bank account at a time
Forecasting in any currency, across different organizations, for multiple time periods
Forecasting cannot combine data from more than one legal entity
questions.explain: Oracle supports multi-currency, multi-org forecasting, letting a single forecast consolidate cash flows across subsidiaries and currencies.

questions.q: Why is a cash forecast described as a 'planning tool, not a guarantee'?
options: Because forecasts are randomly generated with no underlying data
Because open transactions can settle late and historical trends can break, so the actual outcome can differ from the forecast
Because forecasts can only be built once per year
Because forecasting is identical to cash positioning
questions.explain: A forecast depends on assumptions (timely settlement, trend continuation) that can turn out wrong, so it supports planning rather than guaranteeing an exact outcome.
